neighbours.label: the opening quotation mark that introduces a literal gloss or translation of words ('literally "…', 'translated as "…'); quotes that open speech or a title stay low. The + pole of the unit is dictionary-definition text
fire: The Spanish idiom tomar el pelo means, literally, "to take the hair" of someone.
The name of the village is usually translated as "place of many springs" on maps.
The Greek phrase in this verse reads literally "out of faith into faith" here.
The Dutch word gezellig is often rendered as "cosy" but covers much more.
The French expression l'esprit de l'escalier is, literally, "the wit of the staircase" in English.
The old Norse name for the bay can be translated as "smoky inlet" in English.
The Hebrew of the first line says literally "in beginning created God" without an article.
The Chinese title of the film translates literally as "the wind rises again" in English.
quiet: The Spanish waiter laughed and shouted "table for six" across the room.
The name of the village is painted on a sign that says "welcome" in blue.
The priest read the verse aloud and then asked "who will go" in a low voice.
The Dutch band opened the concert with "Morning Light" and played for two hours.
The French teacher wrote on my essay "see me after class" in red ink.
The old captain looked at the bay and muttered "storm by nightfall" to himself.
The rabbi closed the book and whispered "that is enough for today" to the class.
The Chinese restaurant on the corner has a note reading "cash only" by the till.

notes: Card: ' “' x7, ' "' x7, ' ‘' x3, mostly after 'literally' or 'such as' where words are mentioned as words. Probes: 'means, literally, "' 0.50, 'translated as "' 0.55, 'reads literally "' 0.48, 'words such as "' 0.27, 'Greek for "' 0.25, 'means "' 0.21; speech quotes 0.03-0.17, song title 0.04, scare quotes 0.01.
